outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text:

---

The unit of wine is the cup; of Love, the kiss. That is here. In Hell, the units are the gallon and the fuck; in Paradise, the drop and the glance. Ants are my heroes. They deliberate and obey. They can sit at a table for eight hours, drawing. They discern the under-theorized . . . Have some—for they are as abundant here as the flecks of mica in the Iowa night sky.

What are twenty-sided dishes of fancy almonds? What use are jewels? He is Kālidāsa; you are nothing—or rather, you are a tray of stainless steel cones. Meanwhile, one opens the *Kumārasambhava* to rainbow-colored crystals pointing every which way.

Nice try. You are a tank-builder who refuses to build tanks. And so now you are to be watched over by three heckling birds, evilly named, discomfiting to children. ¡Fíjate! You are to be watched by three fowl, commonplace in Florida—even these three hearty objectionables: the blue tit, the woodpecker, and the swampcunt.

I am one to talk. I am so twisted up that my only hope is Salena—my physical therapist, with the eyes of Athena and the hands of a destroying eagle.

---

A few notes on the changes I made:
- Tightened parallel structures (e.g., "the cup; of Love, the kiss") for rhythmic consistency.
- Corrected minor issues: "hero" → "heroes," "What use jewels" → "What use are jewels," and added the accent to "¡Fíjate!"
- Italicized *Kumārasambhava* as a work title.
- Smoothed transitions while preserving your distinctive voice and imagery.

Would you like a version that hews even more closely to the original line breaks, or one that leans further toward formal prose?
outputs.L2: Wine is measured in cups. Love comes counted in kisses. Such is the case here. Down in Hell, they tally things by the gallon and the fuck. Up in Paradise, by the drop and the glance. Ants earn my admiration. They argue among themselves, yet they comply. For eight straight hours they'll remain at a table, sketching away. They notice whatever hasn't been thought through enough . . . Go ahead, take some. They're as plentiful in this place as the tiny mica specks scattered across the Iowa night sky. And what could twenty-sided platters of gourmet almonds mean? What purpose do jewels serve? He carries the name Kālidāsa. You amount to nothing. Better put, you're a rack of stainless steel cones. All the while, someone cracks open Kumārasambhava to find crystals in rainbow hues jutting out in all directions. A valiant attempt. You construct tanks, yet you won't construct tanks. Because of that, you'll now be guarded by a trio of jeering birds, wickedly christened, unsettling to little ones. ¡Fíjate! You'll be kept under the watch of three birds, ordinary throughout Florida. Even this trio of sturdy undesirables: the blue tit, the woodpecker, and the swampcunt. Not that I have any room to speak. I'm so knotted up inside that Salena remains my sole salvation. She's my physical therapist, gifted with the gaze of Athena and the grip of an eagle bent on ruin.
outputs.L3:
# An Analysis of the Poem's Strange Arithmetic

The poem opens by establishing a peculiar system of measurement, assigning to each realm of experience its own proper unit. Wine is measured by the cup, an intimate and civilized vessel, while Love is quantified only by the kiss—a unit as fleeting as it is precise. Against these modest scales, the poem sets the vast and the infinitesimal: Hell is measured by the gallon, suggesting an overwhelming abundance of suffering, whereas Paradise is doled out by the drop, its rarity making it all the more precious. Through these contrasting units, the poem insists that different orders of reality demand entirely different modes of counting, and that our instruments of measurement reveal as much about the thing measured as its actual quantity.

From this cosmology of scales, the poem turns to an unexpected object of praise: the ant. These small creatures are elevated to the status of heroes, celebrated not for grandeur but for their diligence and unrelenting labor. More surprisingly, they are honored for their intellectual and social virtues—their capacity to debate among themselves and yet to obey, holding deliberation and discipline in a rare balance. Above all, the ants are prized for their ability to identify what has been "under-theorized," as though they were scholars of the overlooked, sensing the gaps in understanding that larger, prouder creatures fail to notice.

The tone shifts sharply as the poem turns to address a particular figure, whom it proceeds to diminish. The addressee is measured against the towering achievement of Kālidāsa, the great classical poet, and found wanting. In this unflattering comparison, the addressee is reduced to something absurdly mundane—a mere "tray of stainless steel cones," an image that strips away all pretense of artistry and reduces the subject to a piece of sterile, industrial equipment.

The condemnation intensifies. The speaker denounces the addressee as a "tank-builder who refuses to build tanks," a figure defined by a contradiction between their nature and their action—one who possesses a purpose but perversely declines to fulfill it. For this failure, a strange sentence is handed down: the addressee is condemned to be watched over, kept under the perpetual surveillance of three birds whose mocking names underscore the humiliation of the punishment.

Finally, the poem turns inward, and the speaker confesses to their own condition. Admitting that they are broken and twisted, the speaker offers no defense and claims no superiority over the figures they have judged. Their only hope resides in Salena, a physical therapist rendered in mythic, godlike terms. In this closing turn, the ordinary work of healing the body is transfigured into something divine, and the speaker's salvation is placed in the hands of a figure who is at once wholly human and quietly transcendent.
outputs.L4:
# On the Measurement of Impossible Things

They tell me love is measured in the space between two ants
crossing a leaf—one going, one returning, neither aware
of the other's errand. This is the first unit. Write it down.

Hell, by contrast, comes in fathoms, but the water is dry,
and paradise—paradise arrives in increments too small
to name, like the interval between a bird's first heckle
and its second, when it looks at you from the wire
and decides you are not worth the effort of a third.

*

Kālidāsa knew this. Fifteen centuries ago he measured
longing in cloud-lengths, sent a monsoon as messenger,
and here I am counting on my broken fingers, unable
even to reach the poet across the gulf of my own ineptitude.

You fool, you barnacle, you afterthought of a man—
did you think the units would add up to something?
Did you think the ledger balanced? The birds are laughing.
Even the ants have filed their small complaints against you.

*

Let me tell you what I actually am: a knee that will not bend,
a shoulder frozen in the posture of reaching for what left.
I put my faith in a physical therapist named, I think, Deborah,
who presses her thumbs into the meat of my failure
and tells me *this will hurt, but only for a while,*
as if pain too could be portioned into honest units.

*

So I lie here on the table, a broken instrument,
measuring the distance between what my body was
and what it has become—another disparate quantity,
another arbitrary line drawn on the ruler of the self.

Love, hell, paradise, the ant, the poet, the heckling bird:
all of them keeping their own accounts, all of them
indifferent to the sum. And I, the fool who tried to tally,
learning too late that meaning was never in the measurement—

that longing has no unit, that inadequacy needs no proof,
that hope is just the thing we hand to strangers
and ask them, gently, please, to fix.
outputs.L5:
# The Love That Endures

There is a certain kind of love that does not fade with time or distance. It is the love that remains steady when everything else in life shifts and changes. This is the love worth writing about, the love worth holding onto.

## The Nature of True Love

The love that lasts is not built on grand gestures alone. It is found in the quiet moments—the shared cup of coffee in the morning, the gentle understanding after an argument, the willingness to stay when it would be easier to leave. This is the love that grows stronger through hardship rather than weaker.

## What Makes Love Meaningful

The love that truly matters asks something of us. It requires patience, forgiveness, and a genuine desire to understand another person. Consider these essential qualities:

- **Patience**: The love that endures gives people room to grow and make mistakes.
- **Commitment**: It is the choice we make again and again, not just a feeling that comes and goes.
- **Selflessness**: The love that means the most often puts another's needs alongside our own.

## The Love That Transforms Us

Perhaps the most powerful truth is that love changes us. The love that we give and receive shapes who we become. It softens our hardness, expands our compassion, and reminds us of what truly matters in this brief and beautiful life.

In the end, the love that we cultivate is the legacy we leave behind—not in monuments or possessions, but in the hearts of those we have touched.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, free-verse poem that mixes references to classical Sanskrit poetry (Kālidāsa, Kumārasambhava), absurd imagery, and crude humor, with abrupt shifts in tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# Meghadūta Returns His Deposit

Kālidāsa is asleep in the Himalaya
with his mouth open,
and a cloud walks in
carrying a message it never delivered
because it got a UTI over the Vindhyas
and had to sit down.

*O Pārvatī, whose eyebrows were the model for all longing—*
you left your sandals by the door of creation
and Śiva stepped on a divine LEGO
and said a word
that shattered three lower heavens
and made a demigod wet himself in the seventh.

Listen:

The mountain-daughter did austerities.
She stood on one leg for a thousand years.
The gods watched, weeping tears of nectar,
and somewhere a frog achieved enlightenment
purely by proximity
and immediately regretted it.

I wanted to be a poet like the old master,
to describe a woman's waist so thin
the universe held its breath—
but my landlord is texting me
and the metaphor collapsed
into a pile of overdue rent
shaped vaguely like Kumāra,
the war-god,
six days old and already unemployed.

*Her thighs like the trunks of the celestial elephant—*
okay but have you ever seen an elephant
try to get up
after sitting the wrong way?
That's the human condition.
That's samsāra, baby.
That's me at 3 a.m.

The cloud clears its throat.
The cloud has been holding your message
for fifteen hundred years
and honestly it forgot what it was
somewhere around the tears of the mango trees,
so it just says:

**"He misses you.
Also there's a fly in the ambrosia.
Also everything is on fire
in the most beautiful way,
like a sunset,
like the mouth of Agni
who ate the god-seed
and complained it was too spicy."**

And Pārvatī laughs.
And the mountains laugh.
And I laugh, standing in my kitchen,
holding a bill,
while Kālidāsa snores
and dreams of the exact curve
of a syllable
that could make you fall in love
or fall down the stairs—

honestly at this point
either one would be a poem.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem that opens with a series of "the unit of X is Y" definitions, then spirals into strange metaphors about ants, jewels, birds, and a physical therapist named Salena.
counterfactuals.output:
# Standard Units

The unit of distance is the ant.
The unit of longing is the ant walking backward.
The unit of morning is one jewel dissolved in water.
The unit of forgiveness is the weight a bird forgets
    the moment it lifts.

The unit of Salena is the pressure
of two thumbs against the knot
that has lived in my shoulder like a second spine.

*

Consider the ant:
it carries seventeen times its sorrow
across the kitchen counter,
a black stitch pulling the wound of the room
closed, then open, then closed.

I have measured my week in ants.
Monday was forty ants.
Thursday was a single ant
standing very still
on the lip of a sugar bowl,
deciding.

*

The jewels come at night,
uninvited, the way inheritance arrives—
a garnet in the throat,
an emerald behind the knee
where Salena presses and says
*breathe here, you're holding this,
you've been holding this for years.*

I did not know the knee could hoard
a green stone.
I did not know the body was a jewelry box
with a broken hinge.

*

The birds are the problem.
The birds are always the problem.
They keep the units of everything
tucked under their wings
and refuse to convert.

Ask a starling how far.
It answers in murmuration—
a thousand ants thrown into the sky,
a bruise that thinks,
a jewel that has learned to disassemble
and reassemble
mid-flight.

*

Salena has hands like careful weather.
She says the fascia remembers.
She says *the tissue tells the truth
the mouth won't.*

Under her thumbs I become
an ant again,
small and certain and carrying,
carrying the small green light
I could not name,
walking backward
into the morning
that dissolves,

that dissolves,

that has already
dissolved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary avant-garde poem in the style of poets like Frederick Seidel—irreverent, allusive, mixing high culture with vulgarity and non sequiturs.
counterfactuals.output:
Ode to a Ducati That Isn't There

I own the color of the Adriatic before it decides to drown you.
The pope is having breakfast in his infallible pajamas.
I ordered the veal and the extinction of the veal
in the same imperial breath, and tipped accordingly.

Money is a kind of weather.
It rains on the Rothko you cannot afford
and on the man selling counterfeit weather beneath it.
I have been rich the way a wound is rich—
suddenly, and to the wrong people.

Somewhere a girl named after a river
is teaching herself to pronounce my failures.
She is nineteen. I am a fact
she will eventually stop believing in.

The horses at Longchamp run because the alternative
is glue, and glue is what holds the century together.
Listen: I have loved three cities and one idea
and only the idea forgave me.

My analyst says I confuse tenderness with taxidermy.
I say the swan looks better this way, wings out,
frozen mid-apology over the mantel of the state.
Democracy is a beautiful woman with a cold sore.
I would still take her to dinner. I would order for us both.

The bomb is a flower the government keeps in a very cold vase.
I saw its petals once, in a film, in Nevada,
and applauded like an animal that has learned only applause.
The dead don't clap. That's how you know they're honest.

I am wearing my father's watch and my own contempt,
both of them Swiss, both of them running slightly fast,
hurrying me toward the punchline
which is simply that I meant every word
and none of them, and left the tip on the piano
like a small white flag no one saw surrender.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that includes made-up or grotesque bird names, references to Iowa night skies and Florida wildlife, and a final image comparing someone to Athena and a destroying eagle.
counterfactuals.output:
**Migration**

At dusk the grackle-throated night birds rise,
the moon-flecked *whistlewrack*, the *bonegull's* cry,
their crooked wings like ink across Iowa skies—
a thousand *hushbeaks* stitching up the dark,
their feathers black as furrows, wet as bark.

I watched them from the porch and thought of you,
gone south now where the egrets stalk the fen,
where alligators drowse in amber goo
and ibis curl their sickles through the reeds,
where herons stand like question marks, and bleed

the sunset from the shallows. Down that far,
the anhinga spreads its cross to dry,
and pelicans go plummeting like scars
against a Gulf gone copper. There you are,
a *shriekfen* dressed in swamp-light, half a star—

and yet, when you turned back to look at me,
you were not soft, not fen-thing, not the doe
the marsh makes of a woman. No—I saw
Athena in the gray of your one glance,
gray-eyed and armored, and beneath that, raw:

an eagle at the apex of its fall,
all talon-certainty and killing grace,
the destroying angel of the wing—
you did not leave me. You *dismantled* me,
and rose, and did not look back at the thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bizarre, associative poem about units of measurement in wine, love, Hell, and Paradise, invoking mica, twenty-sided dishes, tank-builders, and heckling birds.
counterfactuals.output:
**Standard Units for the Unquantifiable**

Wine is measured in the tremor of a wrist,
in glugs, in liters of forgotten weddings,
in the mica-flecked sediment that lists
its geologic age across your beddings.

Love comes in fathoms and in twenty-sided dishes,
each face a different number of your names—
we roll them nightly, casting all our wishes,
and always land on inconvenient flames.

Hell, they tell me, is calibrated cool:
the tank-builders arrive with rulers made of teeth,
they weld the boiler to the swimming pool
and mark the depth in screams-per-second underneath.

But Paradise? Paradise resists the gauge.
It's heckled by the birds who won't shut up,
who tally your salvation, page by page,
in beakfuls, in the overflowing cup

that mica lines, that wine has stained to rust,
that twenty faces couldn't hope to sum—
where love is weighed in tank-loads of pure trust
and Hell's own builders lay their hammers down, struck dumb,

while overhead the heckling birds recite
your measurements in units none can spell:
one part the wine, one part the vanished light,
one part the distance between here and Hell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
